claim_text: Electrical connector mating completion can be detected online by combining a relative-displacement model with a force upper bound and multi-sensor monitoring, distinguishing successful completion from jamming faults.
claim_scope: Cross-industry mechanism; PCB board-level connector, lab setup
evidence_extract_or_close_paraphrase: Models completion via relative displacement Δz = z1 − z2 (removing phase shift from initial position error) and a four-phase piecewise-affine force model with an upper force limit F̄. Algorithm 2 declares success when Fz(t) ≥ F̄ and Δz approaches the end point Δẑ, and a jam fault when Fz(t) ≥ F̄ while Δz stays far below Δẑ; force outside set-membership prediction bounds also faults. Sensing combines a wrist force sensor, joint encoders and two CCD cameras (template matching). Experiments (Mitsubishi RV-1A 6-DOF, 5 mm/s): five training samples give four-phase bounds (Table 1); 100 successful samples, about 50 jammed cases (all detected) and 50 gripper-slip faults (quickly detected).
inference_chain: Lab connector-mating completion-monitoring mechanism → bounded R5 completion-criterion analogue
supported_conclusion: Connector mating completion is not a single threshold or single sensor; a relative-displacement PWA model plus a force upper bound and multi-sensor monitoring separates successful completion from jamming faults, supporting R5 as an explicit auditable function.
unsupported_extension_or_transfer_limit: PCB board-level, vertically inserted connectors in a lab setup; not a battery Pack EoL flexible-harness/HV connector, contains no electrical-acceptance check (model is mechanical only), and its five-sample bounds and detection rates do not transfer.
unresolved_evidence_need: Find Pack EoL/equipment electrical-acceptance criteria (lock, continuity, HVIL) and target-station completion-judgment ownership; determine whether mechanical insertion or electrical continuity actually gates completion.
notes: Full text verified via Fuji Press diamond OA (CC BY-ND, JRM Vol.24 No.4, pp.666-676). Backward refs [15] Huang 2008 and [16] Huang 2010 are the older Sasaki/Fukuda-line papers for further chasing.

claim_text: Connector insertion can be completed at human-comparable speed while protecting parts through adaptive impedance control with an online-identified target model and a staged contact-force limit.
claim_scope: Cross-industry mechanism; FA-equipment internal cable connector, dual-robot industrial cell
evidence_extract_or_close_paraphrase: A 6-axis force/moment sensor adjusts the robot command value under impedance control; an LMS algorithm identifies target physical properties (rigidity, attenuation coefficient) online and changes control gain. A staged force limit separates the insertion-start phase (1st limit, reduces force on misalignment so parts are not damaged) from the full-push phase after connector-pin contact (2nd limit). Verification: intentionally displaced insertion positions were corrected in retry, and the system achieved human-comparable assembly time with safe stop under uncompensated positional displacement.
inference_chain: Industrial connector-insertion force control + staged force limit -> bounded G2 force-upper-bound mechanism
supported_conclusion: Adaptive impedance control with an online-identified model and a staged (initiation vs full-push) force limit is an evidenced configuration for protecting connectors and boards while maintaining insertion speed, supporting the force upper bound and safe stop as explicit auditable functions.
unsupported_extension_or_transfer_limit: FA-equipment internal board-level cable connectors in a dual-robot cell under a NEDO project; not a battery Pack EoL flexible-harness/HV connector. The 120 N-class rated sensor, threshold values and cycle-time parity do not transfer to the target task.
unresolved_evidence_need: Identify the target Pack connector's permissible insertion force, whether electrical mating (lock/HVIL) adds a separate acceptance stage, and whether the target station stages its force limit the same way
notes: Full text verified via Fuji Press diamond OA (CC BY-ND, JRM Vol.23 No.6, pp.939-950, 2011). Mitsubishi Electric + Fukuda/Nagoya/Hokkaido/Toyama labs. Self-developed low-cost 6-axis force sensor rated 120 N force / 5 N-m moment, linearity 1.1% RO, resolution 0.2% RO.

claim_text: Connector insertion errors can be automatically detected from a learned force-vs-position abnormality threshold and recovered by selecting among multiple mechanically-motivated search strategies.
claim_scope: Cross-industry mechanism; FA-equipment internal cable connector
evidence_extract_or_close_paraphrase: Error recovery is decomposed into three stages of error detection, error classification and recovery-method selection. Detection focuses on the moment generated by interference between the connector hole and socket pin and compares against an abnormality-determination force threshold derived from force-with-respect-to-position data recorded during successful work. Recovery selection picks among spiral search (contact face enabled, no guaranteed solution), probing search (lateral socket contact, solution guaranteed via error minimization, requires obstacle-free periphery) and binary search (one-dimensional search using connector-inclination height difference, for small holes and clearance) depending on connector shape, socket shape, peripheral space and search time. Verification: intentionally displaced insertion positions were detected and completed in retry operations.
inference_chain: Industrial connector-insertion error-recovery mechanism -> bounded G4 recovery-protocol analogue
supported_conclusion: Automatic connector-insertion recovery can be implemented as a detection-classification-selection pipeline whose detection criterion is a learned force-vs-position abnormality threshold, with multiple search strategies covering different connector geometries; this supports recovery as an auditable configuration function.
unsupported_extension_or_transfer_limit: FA board-level cable connectors in an industrial cell; the specific threshold, search strategies and success rates do not transfer to a battery Pack EoL flexible-harness/HV connector, and the discard-and-retry lost-cable exception has no Pack EoL analogue.
unresolved_evidence_need: Determine the target-station recovery protocol, retry limit, and whether jamming (force high, displacement low) is distinguished from misalignment in the target connector
notes: Complements C026 (S024): both use a force-vs-position-relationship completion/fault criterion, but S031 adds explicit recovery-method selection. Adjacent screw-fixation SVM four-state classification (success/empty/failed/jammed, >97%, Table 1) is a related but non-connector task.

claim_text: Connector pose for insertion can be recognized from 3D sensing with sub-millimetre accuracy, and uncertain recognition can be guarded by repeated re-recognition plus discard-and-retry exception handling.
claim_scope: Cross-industry mechanism; FA-equipment internal cable connector
evidence_extract_or_close_paraphrase: A structured-light 3D sensor (MEMS scanner, under 0.5 kg, 0.1% working-distance-ratio resolution) with a graspability algorithm raises bulk-cable extraction from under 50% to over 90%; connector positioning is computed by chamfer matching over many two-dimensional views of pre-modeled connectors, reaching a mean recognition accuracy of ±0.5 mm in 0.5 s per item with human-comparable extraction/alignment time. Verification: to handle ~10% recognition errors, connectors are re-recognized at multiple angles and a discard-and-pick-another-cable exception keeps the system stable.
inference_chain: Industrial flexible-object perception -> bounded G1 residual-source quantification and mitigation mechanism
supported_conclusion: Sub-millimetre connector-pose recognition combined with re-recognition confirmation and discard-and-retry exception handling is an evidenced way to bound and respond to residual pose uncertainty, supporting residual-source quantification as an auditable capability dimension.
unsupported_extension_or_transfer_limit: FA board-level cable connectors with aligned jig/housing geometry under cell-production conditions; the ±0.5 mm figure is specific to this sensor-and-connector set, not a Pack EoL flexible-harness/HV-connector tolerance statement.
unresolved_evidence_need: Obtain the target Pack connector supplied-pose uncertainty and tolerance relative to pose error, and whether mechanical guiding or vision removes the residual (link to S029 tolerance-vs-robot-error argument)
notes: Recognition accuracy and graspability are configuration-specific, not a universal residual bound. Cross-reference S029 (tolerance vs robot position error) once its full text is verified.

claim_text: A systematic review of 11 collaborative-robotics papers in wire harness assembly confirms that none presents a cost-benefit or cycle-time analysis, leaving the economic and throughput impact of cobot introduction unquantified in this domain.
claim_scope: Secondary evidence; wire-harness assembly (cross-industry analogue for R1), 11 papers
evidence_extract_or_close_paraphrase: Eleven papers were found in the scientific literature. All papers demonstrated the potential of collaborative robots to improve productivity, and two of these addressed ergonomics. None of the papers reviewed presented a cost-benefit or a cycle time analysis to measure the impact of the incorporation of collaborative robots in the wire harness assembly process; this represents an important area of opportunity for research.
inference_chain: Peer-reviewed systematic review of the closest domain -> domain-level gap confirmation
supported_conclusion: The absence of cost-benefit / cycle-time quantification is not merely our own search miss; it is a confirmed gap in the closest reviewed literature on cobots for harness/DLO assembly, so RQ2/RQ3 economic and throughput claims must stay qualitative or scenario-based unless the target task is quantified.
unsupported_extension_or_transfer_limit: Wire-harness assembly, not battery Pack EoL connector handling; it bounds expectations for RQ2/RQ3 but does not itself quantify the target task, and the 'none' statement is scoped to these 11 papers.
unresolved_evidence_need: Confirm the review's coverage window and search method; treat as a domain-level gap (11 papers), not a universal null result across all robotics
notes: Full text verified via MDPI gold OA (CC BY, Robotics 11(3):65, 2022). Note: distinct from the 2022-11 case study 10.3390/robotics11060131 by the same lead author.

claim_text: In reviewed harness-assembly cobot work, robotized tasks cluster on spot-taping, cable routing, wire insertion, cable-tie collocation and adhesive taping, while connector mating is only mentioned as an adjacent task without dedicated study; three papers emphasize computer vision for cross-harness versatility.
claim_scope: Secondary evidence; wire-harness assembly closest-work map
evidence_extract_or_close_paraphrase: Reviewed tasks concentrate on spot-taping (Gualtieri, Ibanez, Sugiono), cable-routing, wire insertion, cable-tie collocation and adhesive taping; connector mating appears only alongside cable-routing as a listed task. Three papers (Nguyen & Yoon, Kicki, Yumbla) apply computer vision to identify harnesses or connector terminals and adapt to different harness types, reducing reprogramming.
inference_chain: Peer-reviewed review task map -> closest-work inventory for R1, showing connector mating is thin
supported_conclusion: Connector mating is an under-covered task in existing harness-assembly cobot research (spot-taping and routing dominate), supporting our treatment of connector adaptation as an under-evidenced contact-layer task rather than a solved reference.
unsupported_extension_or_transfer_limit: Battery Pack EoL test-connector handling lies outside this review; the task map is a cross-industry analogue and does not include a test (as opposed to assembly) connector-mating analysis.
unresolved_evidence_need: Retrieve and verify the specific connector-mating mention and whether any reviewed paper addresses a test-side (not assembly-side) connector mating
notes: Same review as C030. The 'cable-routing and mating electric connectors' phrase is a single task listing in Section 2, not an analyzed case.

claim_text: A configured cobot cell (Universal Robots UR5 + OnRobot RG2 gripper + Cognex IS7905M vision) performs cable-tie collocation on a wire-harness board; vision detects board holes and passes their positions to the cobot via Modbus, letting the cell adapt to different harness types without reprogramming.
claim_scope: Cross-industry analogue mechanism (wire-harness assembly, not battery Pack EoL)
evidence_extract_or_close_paraphrase: The collaborative robot UR5 with an RG2 gripper and a Cognex IS7905M camera performs cable-tie collocation; the camera identifies holes on the harness board and positions are sent to the cobot through Modbus, with movement programmed in Polyscope. The vision system allows working with different types and forms of wire harnesses without changing the cobot programming.
inference_chain: Configured robot + vision -> object-state perception and adaptability, but gripper/placement correctness unverified
supported_conclusion: A cobot + vision configuration can localize a flexible harness-board object and adapt across harness variants without reprogramming, a concrete mechanism for the contact-layer object-state function.
unsupported_extension_or_transfer_limit: Not battery Pack EoL; the gripper was NOT developed and collocation correctness was NOT assessed, so this is prototype/simulation-level evidence. The human still places the harness body on the board to avoid the difficulty cobots have with flexible materials.
unresolved_evidence_need: Whether a production-ready gripper and placement verification would preserve the claimed adaptation; no battery-level transfer argument exists
notes: Full text verified via MDPI gold OA (CC BY, Robotics 11(6):131, 2022-11-16). Sister case-study to review S033 (same lead author).

claim_text: The cobot-supported cable-tie cell quantifies an ergonomic improvement for the assembly worker (RULA from 7 to 4; JSI from 12 to 4.5), grounding a non-economic benefit of cobot introduction while cost and cycle time remain unquantified.
evidence_extract_or_close_paraphrase: Without the cobot the task scored RULA 7 (urgent changes required) and JSI 12 (dangerous); with the cobot the scores reduced to RULA 4 and JSI 4.5 (below the maximum acceptable risk). The work is an early prototype and simulation; the gripper was not developed and the correctness of cable-tie collocation was not assessed.
inference_chain: Quantified ergonomic benefit -> one RQ2 dimension has quantified evidence; economic/throughput dimension still absent (consistent with C030)
supported_conclusion: Ergonomics is the one dimension in this closest cobot-for-harness case with a quantitative result, confirming that cost/cycle-time quantification is the recurring absence across the closest literature.
unsupported_extension_or_transfer_limit: Early prototype and simulation, not a production deployment; ergonomic scores are task- and setup-specific and not transferable to battery Pack EoL.
unresolved_evidence_need: Any independent reproduction; production-grade deployment and non-ergonomic (cost / cycle-time) quantification
notes: Same source as C032. RULA/JSI values confirm a quantified ergonomic benefit, reinforcing S033's finding that economic/throughput analysis is absent.
